clinicalPearls: A pure motor palsy of the posterior interosseous nerve, the deep motor branch of the radial nerve, most often entrapped at the arcade of Frohse (the proximal fibrous edge of supinator) within the radial tunnel
The hallmark is finger drop with loss of metacarpophalangeal extension of the fingers and thumb, but with PRESERVED wrist extension and NO sensory loss because the superficial radial nerve is spared
Wrist extension deviates radially because extensor carpi radialis longus (innervated proximal to the branch) is preserved while extensor carpi ulnaris is weak
Common causes include a proximal mass such as a lipoma or ganglion, rheumatoid synovitis of the elbow, radial tunnel fibrous bands, and trauma including Monteggia fracture-dislocation

It must be distinguished from radial tunnel syndrome, which causes pain over the mobile wad without motor deficit, and from extensor tendon rupture, differentiated by the tenodesis test showing intact tendons

Onset may be gradual and painless in entrapment, or acute and painful, in which case inflammatory neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner) affecting the posterior interosseous nerve should be considered

Management is initially conservative with splinting and observation for compressive or inflammatory cases, with surgical exploration and decompression indicated for a structural lesion or failure to recover
reference.pathophysiology: After the radial nerve divides at the level of the elbow, the posterior interosseous nerve passes into the radial tunnel and dives between the two heads of supinator, most commonly compressed at the proximal fibrous margin known as the arcade of Frohse. Because this branch is purely motor, distal to the take-off of extensor carpi radialis longus and the superficial radial sensory nerve, entrapment produces selective weakness of the digital and thumb extensors, extensor carpi ulnaris and the radial abductors of the thumb, without sensory loss. Compression from fibrous bands, a space-occupying mass, proliferative synovitis or trauma causes focal demyelination and, if sustained, axonal loss; the preserved extensor carpi radialis longus explains the radial deviation on attempted wrist extension.
additionalDifferentials: Radial tunnel syndrome (pain without motor weakness)
Extensor tendon rupture, for example in rheumatoid arthritis
Main radial nerve palsy (which includes wrist drop and sensory loss)
Neuralgic amyotrophy involving the posterior interosseous nerve
Sagittal band rupture causing extensor tendon subluxation
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of posterior interosseous-innervated muscles with sparing of extensor carpi radialis longus and brachioradialis
Tenodesis test to confirm extensor tendon integrity and exclude rupture
High-resolution ultrasound of the radial tunnel to identify a mass or focal nerve change
MRI of the elbow and proximal forearm to detect lipoma, ganglion or synovitis
Plain radiographs if Monteggia fracture-dislocation or bony abnormality is suspected
Inflammatory markers and rheumatoid serology when synovitis is considered
redFlags: Acute severe pain preceding weakness, suggesting neuralgic amyotrophy
A palpable or imaging-detected mass in the proximal forearm
Progressive weakness despite conservative treatment indicating a structural compressive lesion
Antecedent Monteggia fracture-dislocation or elbow trauma
reference.prognosis: Compressive lesions treated by removing or decompressing the offending structure, and inflammatory cases, commonly recover good extensor function, although recovery may take several months. Long-standing entrapment with axonal loss recovers less completely and may require tendon transfer to restore digital extension.
pitfalls: Mistaking finger drop for extensor tendon rupture without performing the tenodesis test
Diagnosing a full radial nerve palsy when wrist extension and sensation are in fact preserved
Overlooking a proximal forearm mass such as a lipoma or ganglion as the cause
Failing to consider neuralgic amyotrophy in acute painful presentations
Confusing the painless motor syndrome with painful radial tunnel syndrome, which lacks true weakness
management: Treat identified compressive lesions by excising a mass such as a lipoma or ganglion, or surgically decompressing fibrous bands at the arcade of Frohse
Address underlying rheumatoid synovitis of the elbow with disease-modifying antirheumatic therapy and synovectomy where relevant
Trial conservative management with activity modification, splinting and physiotherapy in mild or early entrapment without a mass
Manage suspected inflammatory neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner) with analgesia and consider corticosteroids, allowing spontaneous recovery
Provide hand therapy with dynamic extension splinting to maintain function while awaiting reinnervation
Monitor recovery with serial examination and electrophysiology, recognising that reinnervation may take several months
Refer for tendon transfer to restore finger and thumb extension when long-standing axonal loss precludes recovery
